tagline.text: A Dagupan city beach with Lingayen Gulf sunsets and MacArthur's landing site

location.label: Location
location.text: Tondaligan Road, Bonuan Gueset, Dagupan City, Pangasinan

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,200 (per person for a half day on site, excluding transport)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Clark International Airport (CRK), then by road

children.text: Tondaligan Blue Beach is an urban beach on Lingayen Gulf in the Bonuan district of Dagupan City, set inside the 72-hectare Tondaligan People's Park. Fine gray sand, a long baywalk, gulf sunsets and the history of the 1945 American landing make it an easy family outing.

Tondaligan Blue Beach lies on the northern coast of Dagupan City, Pangasinan, in the Bonuan Gueset district. Locals also call it Bonuan Blue Beach or simply Tondaligan Beach. Facing Lingayen Gulf, it is surrounded by the roughly 72-hectare Tondaligan People's Park, and because it is close to the city center it is the go-to urban beach where local families bring packed lunches on weekends.
The name "Blue Beach" comes from a World War II military code name. On
January 9, 1945

, the first combat troops of the US Sixth Army, under General Douglas MacArthur, landed on this shore to begin the liberation of Luzon. As a result, the area now includes memorial spaces such as the MacArthur Landing Park and a Philippine-Japanese friendship park. A walk through this history makes the visit much richer than just a swim and a trip home.

The sand is not white but fine and grayish. If you expect the white sand of Boracay or of Pangasinan's other beaches, you may be disappointed. In return, the shoreline is long and the water deepens gently, which is good for children playing at the water's edge, and because the gulf opens to the west, the sky turning red at dusk is the beach's biggest attraction. The baywalk, which runs for several kilometers along the shore, fills with joggers and cyclists in the morning and evening.

Visitor opinions are mixed. Review sites carry comments that complain about the restrooms and holiday crowds as well as comments that say the city's cleanup has made the beach cleaner than before. In short, think of it not as a glamorous resort but as a modest outing where you enjoy the sea, the sunset and some history close to downtown Dagupan, and you will leave satisfied.

Because the gulf opens to the west, the sky turns orange and red at dusk. According to local guides, the most beautiful time is roughly between 5:15 PM and 6:00 PM, when people gather on the baywalk to watch. The time of sunset changes with the season, so get a spot early.

The sand is fine and grayish, and the water deepens gradually. In the dry season the water is a relatively clear gray-blue. It is good for children playing in waist-deep water, but waves can get high on some days, so an adult should always keep watch.

A paved promenade and bike lane run for a long stretch along the coast. Before 8 AM it is mostly joggers and cyclists, so it is quiet, while at midday the sun is strong and there is little shade. It is a good way to take in the whole beach on foot.
Because this is the Blue Beach where American troops landed on
January 9, 1945
, there are a MacArthur Landing Park and a Philippine-Japanese friendship park nearby. They are close to the beach and can be visited on foot. Exhibits and opening hours may change, so check locally.

Rows of cottages with shade and tables stand in front of the beach, and families and groups can rent one to eat and rest. Cottages are for day use only, with no overnight stays. On holidays the rates go up and the cottages fill fast, so go early.

The park has a children's playground and a Japanese-style garden, and there are cafes and restaurants near the beach. Even if the sand is not to your taste, the children have somewhere to play, which makes this a fine family outing.

blocks.title: Snacks and grilled food by the beach

children.text: Small stalls on the beach sell cold drinks and simple foods such as charcoal-grilled dishes, skewers and pancit canton. Dagupan is famous as the "bangus (milkfish) capital," so grilled bangus dishes are also easy to find in restaurants in town.
It is said that you can negotiate a bangka at the Tondaligan Boat Yard to reach Pugaro Island. One trip is said to take about
15–20 minutes
, but check the fare, life jackets and whether boats are running directly on site.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: Afternoon swim and sunset, dinner in town

children.text: From the Dagupan bus terminal, take a tricycle or jeepney to Tondaligan. It is easiest to get off near the "I ♥ Tondaligan" sign at the beach entrance.
Rent a cottage and leave your things there, and split the fee if your group has 6 to 8 people. Bring coins for the restroom and showers.
Swim in an area where swimming is allowed. Stay in the zone with lifeguards, and if you are told to leave the water late in the afternoon, follow that advice.
Walk the baywalk and look around the MacArthur Landing Park area. It is also a good time to let the children play at the playground.
Watch the sunset from a good spot on the beach or the baywalk. When the sky turns red, it is a great time for photos.
Head back into the city and have dinner at a restaurant on Galvan Street, trying pigar-pigar or bangus dishes.

On holidays the cottages and parking fill early, so it is better to arrive in the morning. In that case you can change the plan to a baywalk stroll and swim in the morning, lunch at the cottage, and a return to the city in the afternoon.

items.title: Full-day course
items.subtitle: From a morning walk to a visit to Pugaro Island

children.text: Arrive early and take a spot without worrying about parking. At this hour many joggers are out and it is quiet.
Take a morning walk or ride a bike along the baywalk. Walking the whole beach takes roughly
40 minutes–1 hour
Rent a cottage, buy snacks at the beach stalls and go for a swim. The midday sun is strong, so you need a hat and sunscreen.
Have lunch with food you brought to the cottage or with food from the beach stalls. Dagupan is known for bangus, so eating at a restaurant in town is also good.
Ask about a bangka at the Tondaligan Boat Yard and check locally whether a visit to Pugaro Island is possible. If the weather is bad, do not push it.
Return to the beach, watch the sunset, and then head into the city.

Manila to Dagupan is about 220–230 km. Buses to Dagupan leave from Cubao for Five Star and Dagupan Bus, from Pasay for Victory Liner, and from PITX for Solid North. Schedules change, so check with the operator.
Travel time is roughly
5–6 hours
depending on traffic, and fares for air-conditioned buses are listed at roughly
. Fuel surcharges may raise them.
After getting off at the Dagupan bus terminal, continue to the beach using the local transport described below.
Bus fares and travel times differ by source, so only approximate ranges are given. Ask each operator for the latest fares.

items.title: By car or rental car from Manila

children.text: Take NLEX, SCTEX and TPLEX, exit at Urdaneta or Dagupan, and follow the coastal road to the Tondaligan parking area. With reasonable traffic it takes roughly
4–5 hours
Expressway tolls are listed at roughly
one way. Roads get congested on holidays, so allow extra time.

items.title: From the city to the beach

children.text: From the Dagupan bus terminal, take a jeepney bound for Bonuan or Tondaligan, or use a tricycle. A shared tricycle is listed at about
per person and a whole tricycle at about
. Agree on the fare before you ride.
Grab is also available in Dagupan city.

The dry season from November to May is a good time to visit. November to February in particular is relatively cool with calm waves, which suits first-time visitors. March to May is the hottest and busiest peak season, and in April, when the Bangus Festival takes place, it is wise to book accommodation early.
During the rainy season from June to October, waves get higher and the water turns murky, and from September to October there is a chance of typhoons. Check PAGASA advisories and avoid swimming then.

There is not much lodging right in front of the beach. A small hotel stands near the beach, but most accommodation is in Dagupan city. Budget lodging is listed at roughly
per night and mid-range at roughly
, but this changes with the season, so check on a booking site.

Dagupan is famous for bangus (milkfish). In restaurants in town you can eat dishes such as grilled bangus, boneless fried daing and sinigang, and on Galvan Street there are restaurants selling pigar-pigar, stir-fried pork offal. At the beach, it is easiest to eat lightly from the stalls.
On holidays and in peak season, arrive in the morning to find parking and a cottage more easily.
The sand is not white, so do not expect too much; think of it as an outing combining sunset, a walk and some history.
Bring coins for the restroom and showers.
There is little shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and plenty of water.
Water shoes are a good idea so you do not step on sea urchins or sharp objects in the water.
Agree on the tricycle fare before you ride or check the meter.
Bring mosquito repellent.
The baywalk is a good place for sunset photos, and it is easier to return to the city for dinner.

Whether swimming is allowed, the hours, and lifeguard coverage change with the weather and with the city. In the rainy and typhoon seasons there are rip currents and high waves, so follow local advice. Super Typhoon Uwan in November 2025 wrecked cottages and toppled the lifeguard tower, and swimming and leisure activities were banned for a time, so check the city's advisory on repair and reopening status before you go.
There is guidance that currents become irregular around sunset, so late in the afternoon follow the advice to leave the water.
From June to October there may be rip currents and big waves. If you are caught in a rip current, swim parallel to the shore and then angle back.
There is little shade and the midday sun is strong.

Jellyfish can increase. Over the April 2026 Easter holiday dozens of people were stung in a day and swimming was suspended for a day, and they may also increase from August to October. If stung, calmly leave the water, tell a lifeguard or medical team, and go to a clinic if you have trouble breathing.
When boarding a bangka, check that there is a life jacket for every person, and postpone if the weather is bad.
Do not leave valuables in the cottage or on the beach.
It is inside the beach area, a few minutes on foot, and shows the history of the 1945 landing.
